title: Risotto con Zucca
subtitle: Butternut squash risotto with Parmesan and nutmeg
excerpt: Risotto con zucca is a sweet, golden risotto made with roasted butternut squash, Parmesan, and a little nutmeg. It is a Venetian and Mantuan autumn dish. Half the squash is roasted and pureed into the risotto for colour and depth; the other half is left in soft cubes for texture.
sourceNotes: Pumpkin and squash risotto (risotto alla zucca) is a classic of the Veneto and Lombardy, particularly around Mantua where the local cucurbita di Mantova is used. The technique of pureeing part of the squash into the risotto base is standard across the region.

content.text: The key move in squash risotto is roasting the squash first rather than simmering it in the stock. Roasting concentrates the flavour and slightly caramelises the edges. Half is mashed or pureed into the soffritto before the rice is added; this turns the whole risotto golden and gives it a sweet depth.

Preheat the oven to 200C. Toss {{butternut-squash}} squash cubes with 1 tbsp of the olive oil and {{salt-table}} of the salt. Spread on a roasting tin and roast for 25 minutes until tender and golden at the edges. Set aside half the squash cubes. Mash or puree the other half.
Heat the remaining {{extra-virgin-olive-oil}} olive oil in a heavy pan over medium heat. Add {{onion}} onion and cook for 8 minutes until soft. Stir in the pureed squash and cook for 2 minutes.

Add {{carnaroli-rice}} rice and stir for 2 minutes. Pour in {{white-wine-dry}} wine and stir until absorbed. Add hot {{vegetable-stock}} stock a ladleful at a time for 18 minutes until the rice is al dente.
Stir in {{unsalted-butter}} butter, {{parmesan}} Parmesan, {{nutmeg}} nutmeg, and the roasted squash cubes. Season with {{salt-table}} remaining salt and {{black-pepper}} pepper. Serve at once.

items.symptom: The risotto tastes bland despite the squash
items.cause: The squash was steamed rather than roasted, losing its caramelised depth.
items.fix: Roasting is essential. Squash needs dry heat to develop flavour. Do not skip the oven step or substitute steamed squash.

content.text: Squash risotto is particularly associated with Mantua and the lower Po valley, where large, sweet cucurbite have been grown since the sixteenth century. In Mantua, pumpkin risotto is sometimes finished with crushed amaretti biscuits and mostarda, which adds a sweet-sharp contrast. This version is the simpler, more widely made form found across northern Italy in autumn.
